claim: TCR repertoires encode clinically valuable information that reflects prior antigen exposure and potential future response.
source: T-cell receptors (TCRs) encode clinically valuable information that reflects prior antigen exposure and potential future response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Enormous TCR diversity complicates the use of TCR clonotypes as clinical biomarkers.
source: However, despite advances in deep repertoire sequencing, enormous TCR diversity complicates the use of TCR clonotypes as clinical biomarkers.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the abstract.

claim: The study generated 1831 public TCR meta-clonotypes from SARS-CoV-2 antigen-associated TCRs with strong evidence of HLA restriction.
source: We apply the framework to TCR data from COVID-19 patients, generating 1831 public TCR meta-clonotypes from the SARS-CoV-2 antigen-associated TCRs that have strong evidence of restriction to patients with a specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Meta-clonotypes targeting specific epitopes were more frequently detected in bulk repertoires compared to exact amino acid matches.
source: Applied to independent cohorts, meta-clonotypes targeting these specific epitopes were more frequently detected in bulk repertoires compared to exact amino acid matches
evidence: This is a key result stated in the abstract.

claim: 59.7% (1093/1831) of meta-clonotypes were more abundant among COVID-19 patients that expressed the putative restricting HLA allele (FDR<0.01).
source: 59.7% (1093/1831) were more abundant among COVID-19 patients that expressed the putative restricting HLA allele (false discovery rate [FDR]<0.01)
evidence: This is a quantitative result stated in the abstract.

claim: An individual's unique repertoire of TCRs is shaped by antigen exposure and is a critical component of immunological memory.
source: An individual's unique repertoire of T-cell receptors (TCRs) is shaped by antigen exposure and is a critical component of immunological memory (Emerson et al., 2017; Welsh and Selin, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TCR repertoires are a largely untapped source of biomarkers that could potentially be used to predict immune responses to viral infections, tumor neoantigens, or environmental allergens.
source: With the advancement of immune repertoire profiling, TCR repertoires are a largely untapped source of biomarkers that could potentially be used to predict immune responses to a wide range of exposures including viral infections (Wolf et al., 2018), tumor neoantigens (Ahmadzadeh et al., 2019; Chiou et al., 2021; Kato et al., 2018), or environmental allergens (Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Many distinct TCRs are able to recognize even a single pMHC.
source: Using peptide—major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) tetramer sorting to focus on TCRs recognizing individual epitopes, which depends on knowing the peptide antigen and its MHC restriction, typically reveals that many distinct TCRs are able to recognize even a single pMHC (Coles et al., 2020; Meysman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Only 10–15% of single-chain TCRs are public or shared by multiple individuals.
source: Modeling (Elhanati et al., 2018) and empirical evidence (Soto et al., 2019) suggest that only 10–15% of single-chain TCRs are public or shared by multiple individuals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling and empirical studies.

claim: Individual T-cell clonotypes are currently suboptimal and underpowered for population-level investigations of TCR specificity.
source: Thus, individual T-cell clonotypes are currently suboptimal and underpowered for population-level investigations of TCR specificity, which limits their application in the development of TCR-based clinical biomarkers.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the challenges described.

claim: TCRdist is a biochemically informed distance metric that enabled grouping of paired αβ TCRs by antigen specificity based on their sequence similarity.
source: Previously, we introduced TCRdist, a biochemically informed distance metric that enabled grouping of paired αβ TCRs by antigen specificity based on their sequence similarity (Dash et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: TCRdist is correlated with edit distance, but it can vary considerably among TCRs with identical edit distances.
source: TCRdist is correlated with edit distance, but it can vary considerably among TCRs with identical edit distances (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2.

claim: The MIRA antigen stimulation assays identified 253 sets of 6 or more TCR β-chains associated with CD8+ T cells activated by exposure to SARS-CoV-2 peptides.
source: The MIRA antigen stimulation assays identified 253 sets of 6 or more TCR β-chains associated with CD8+ T cells activated by exposure to SARS-CoV-2 peptides, with TCR sets analyzed ranging in size from 6 to 16,607 TCRs (Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: This is a description of the data analyzed in the study.

claim: In 10,000 β-chain TCRs from an umbilical cord blood sample, less than 1% of TCR amino acid sequences were observed more than once.
source: For example, in 10,000 β-chain TCRs from an umbilical cord blood sample, less than 1 % of TCR amino acid sequences were observed more than once, inclusive of possible clonal expansions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: 45% of amino acid TCR sequences were observed more than once in a set of influenza M1(GILGFVFTL)-A*02:01 peptide–MHC tetramer-sorted subrepertoires from 15 subjects.
source: For instance, 45% of amino acid TCR sequences were observed more than once (excluding clonal expansions) in a set of influenza M1(GILGFVFTL)-A*02:01 peptide–MHC tetramer-sorted subrepertoires from 15 subjects (Dash et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The proportion of unique TCRs with at least one biochemically similar neighbor is higher among sets of antigen-associated TCRs compared to background repertoires.
source: As the radius about a TCR centroid expands, the number of TCRs it encompasses naturally increases. The increase was greater among the sets of antigen-associated TCRs compared to the 'background' repertoires that were not experimentally enriched for antigen-specific T cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Many TCRs within tetramer-enriched repertoires have empty or sparse neighborhoods even at a radius of 24 tdus.
source: Notably there were also many TCRs with empty or sparse neighborhoods using a radius of 12 tdus (111/247, 44%) or 24 tdus (83/247, 34%).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the analysis.

claim: TCRs within sparse neighborhoods represent uncommon modes of antigen recognition.
source: This suggests that TCRs within sparse neighborhoods represent uncommon modes of antigen recognition and highlights the broad heterogeneity of neighborhood densities even among TCRs recognizing a single peptide–MHC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: TCRs with sparse or empty neighborhoods tended to have longer CDR3 loops.
source: We also noted that TCRs with sparse or empty neighborhoods tended to have longer CDR3 loops (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: TCRs with sparse or empty neighborhoods tended to have lower generation probability (pgen).
source: We also noted that TCRs with sparse or empty neighborhoods tended to have longer CDR3 loops (Figure 4C) and lower generation of probability (pgen; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: TCRs with longer CDR3 loops have a lower pgen during genomic recombination of the TCR locus.
source: This is consistent with mathematical modeling that shows that TCRs with longer CDR3 loops have a lower pgen during genomic recombination of the TCR locus (Marcou et al., 2018; Murugan et al., 2012; Sethna et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: For each TCR in the MIRA55:ORF1ab dataset, its radius-defined meta-clonotype was more abundant within a repertoire and more prevalent in a human cohort than the exact clonotype.
source: We found that for each TCR, its radius-defined meta-clonotype was more abundant within a repertoire and more prevalent in a human cohort than the exact clonotype
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: TCR meta-clonotypes formed from the MIRA55:ORF1ab TCR set were detected in 3–12 (median 6) of 15 HLA-A*01 participants in the MIRA cohort.
source: for example, TCR meta-clonotypes formed from the MIRA55:ORF1ab TCR set were detected in 3–12 (median 6) of 15 HLA-A*01 participants in the MIRA cohort, despite 34 of the 46 centroid clonotype TCRs being private (i.e., found in only 1 of 15 HLA-A*01 participants) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis, supported by Figure 6.

claim: The optimal radius for meta-clonotype definition depends on the size of the synthetic background used.
source: We found that with a smaller background the optimal radius tended to be greater and was more variable over repeat samples
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: As the size of the background increased to 1,000,000 the estimates of the optimal radius generally approached the estimate using a 2,000,000 TCR background.
source: As the size of the background increased to 1,000,000 the estimates of the optimal radius generally approached the estimate using a 2,000,000 TCR background (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis, supported by Figure 7.

claim: The MIRA antigen stimulation assays used to generate the IMMUNEcode 2.0 database identified sets of TCR β-chains associated with recognition of a SARS-CoV-2 antigen using CD8+ T cells enriched from PBMC samples from 62 COVID-19 diagnosed patients and 26 COVID-19-negative subjects.
source: The MIRA antigen stimulation assays used to generate the IMMUNEcode 2.0 database (Nolan et al., 2020) identified sets of TCR β-chains associated with recognition of a SARS-CoV-2 antigen using CD8+ T cells enriched from PBMC samples from 62 COVID-19 diagnosed patients and 26 COVID-19-negative subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the data source, supported by citation.

claim: From 91,122 TCR β-clonotypes across 97 MIRA sets, the study engineered 4548 public meta-clonotypes.
source: From 91,122 TCR β-clonotypes across these 97 MIRA sets – targeting antigens in ORF1ab (n = 35), S (n = 27), N (n = 10), M (n = 7), ORF3a (n = 7), ORF7a (n = 4), E (n = 2), ORF8 (n = 2), ORF6 (n = 1), ORF7b (n = 1), and ORF10 (n = 1) – we engineered 4548 public meta-clonotypes
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The 4548 public meta-clonotypes spanned 15% (13,949/91,122) of the original TCR sequences.
source: which spanned 15 % (13,949/91,122) of the original TCR sequences (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: 17 of the 252 MIRA sets showed strong evidence of HLA-A or HLA-B restriction based on computational prediction of HLA binding and enrichment of an HLA among participants contributing to the MIRA TCRs.
source: We found that for 17 of the MIRA sets, the patients contributing TCRs were significantly enriched for at least 1 HLA-A or HLA-B allele (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.001) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: A positive HLA association (FDR <0.01) was detected for 51.5% (943/1831) of the meta-clonotypes using the RADIUS definition.
source: Across all MIRA sets, a positive HLA association (FDR <0.01) was detected for 51.5 % (943/1831) and 59.7 % (1093/1831) of the meta-clonotypes using the RADIUS or RADIUS + MOTIF definitions, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: A positive HLA association (FDR <0.01) was detected for 59.7% (1093/1831) of the meta-clonotypes using the RADIUS + MOTIF definition.
source: Across all MIRA sets, a positive HLA association (FDR <0.01) was detected for 51.5 % (943/1831) and 59.7 % (1093/1831) of the meta-clonotypes using the RADIUS or RADIUS + MOTIF definitions, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: An HLA association (FDR <0.01) was detected for fewer than 3.7% (69/1831) of EXACT centroid features.
source: In comparison, an HLA association (FDR <0.01) was detected for fewer than 3.7 % (69/1831) of EXACT centroid features, largely because the specific TRBV gene and CDR3 sequences discovered in the MIRA experiments were infrequently observed in bulk-sequenced samples (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: The abundance of centroid TCRs in bulk repertoires tended to be positively associated with expression of the restricting HLA allele when detectable.
source: When detectable, the abundance of centroid TCRs in bulk repertoires tended to be positively associated with expression of the restricting HLA allele, as hypothesized.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: The FDR-adjusted q values of associations for centroid TCRs were orders of magnitude larger (less statistically significant) than those obtained from using the engineered RADIUS or RADIUS + MOTIF feature with the same clonotype as a centroid.
source: However, in most cases, the associated FDR-adjusted q value of these associations were orders of magnitude larger (i.e., less statistically significant) than those obtained from using the engineered RADIUS or RADIUS + MOTIF feature with the same clonotype as a centroid (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, supported by Figure 9.

claim: The regression models with meta-clonotypes revealed possible negative associations between TCR abundance and participant age.
source: Moreover, the regression models with meta-clonotypes also revealed possible negative associations between TCR abundance and participant age and positive associations with sample collection more than 2 days post-COVID-19 diagnosis (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, supported by Figure 9A.

claim: The regression models with meta-clonotypes revealed positive associations between TCR abundance and sample collection more than 2 days post-COVID-19 diagnosis.
source: Moreover, the regression models with meta-clonotypes also revealed possible negative associations between TCR abundance and participant age and positive associations with sample collection more than 2 days post-COVID-19 diagnosis (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis, supported by Figure 9A.

claim: Only antigen-associated TCRs with high probability of generation (pgen) are likely to be detected reliably across individuals.
source: Given the extent of TCR diversity, only antigen-associated TCRs with high probability of generation (pgen) are likely to be detected reliably across individuals (Figure 13).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion, supported by Figure 13.

claim: Using exact matching, only associations with high probability of generation antigen-specific TCRs are likely to be detected reliably.
source: Using exact matching, only associations with high probability of generation (pgen) antigen-specific T-cell receptors (TCRs) are likely to be detected reliably.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 13 caption.

claim: Using meta-clonotypes, tcrdist3 revealed strong evidence of HLA-restriction for TCRs with both high and low probability of generation.
source: However, using meta-clonotypes, tcrdist3 revealed strong evidence of HLA-restriction for TCRs with both high and low probability of generation.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 13 caption.

claim: Significant confirmatory evidence of HLA restriction of meta-clonotype abundance was found for 11/17 (64%) of the MIRA sets analyzed.
source: Overall, we found significant confirmatory evidence of the HLA restriction of meta-clonotype abundance for a majority of the MIRA sets we analyzed (11/17, 64%)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Significant confirmatory evidence of HLA restriction was found for 1080/1831 (59%) of the individual meta-clonotypes tested using the RADIUS + MOTIF approach.
source: and for a majority (1080/1831, 59%) of the individual meta-clonotypes tested using the RADIUS + MOTIF approach
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: There were no meta-clonotypes significantly associated with the absence of expression of the restricting HLA allele.
source: importantly, there were no meta-clonotypes significantly associated with the absence of expression of the restricting HLA allele.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: Both tcrdist3 meta-clonotypes and GLIPH2-identified TCR groups were more strongly associated with the predicted A*01 HLA restriction than exact clonotypes for MIRA55:ORF1ab.
source: MIRA55:ORF1ab is an illustrative example; both the tcrdist3 meta-clonotypes and GLIPH2-identified TCR groups were more strongly associated with the predicted A*01 HLA restriction than exact clonotypes
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison analysis.

claim: Meta-clonotypes often subsume multiple GLIPH2 groups.
source: Inspection of the meta-clonotypes and GLIPH2 groups showed that they were often overlapping, with meta-clonotypes subsuming multiple GLIPH2 groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison analysis.

claim: The motif constraints of the meta-clonotypes were able to match a broader set of antigen-specific CDR3s compared to any one GLIPH2 specificity pattern.
source: These observations suggest that the motif constraints of the meta-clonotypes were able to match a broader set of antigen-specific CDR3s compared to any one GLIPH2 specificity pattern, which may have helped boost detection sensitivity in the COVID-19 repertoires.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison results.

claim: tcrdist3 is an open-source Python3 package for TCR repertoire analysis and visualization.
source: To enable TCR biomarker development and innovative extensions of distance-based immune repertoire analysis, we developed tcrdist3, which provides open-source (https://github.com/kmayerb/tcrdist3), documented (https://tcrdist3.readthedocs.io) computational building blocks for a wide array of TCR repertoire workflows in Python3.
evidence: This is a description of the software developed in the study.

claim: Identification of meta-clonotypes from the MIRA55:ORF1ab dataset (n = 479 TCRs) was completed in less than 5 min using 2 CPUs and <4 GB of memory.
source: as a reference, identification of meta-clonotypes from the MIRA55:ORF1ab dataset (n = 479 TCRs) was completed in less than 5 min using 2 CPUs and <4 GB of memory including distance computation and radius optimization.
evidence: This is a performance benchmark for the software.

claim: Quantification of the identified meta-clonotypes (n = 40) conformant TCRs in 694 bulk β-chain repertoires could be completed in less than 2 hr using 2 CPUs and <6 GB memory.
source: Quantification of the identified meta-clonotypes (n = 40) conformant TCRs in 694 bulk β-chain repertoires, ranging in size from 10,395 to 1,038,012 in-frame clones (~5 billion total pairwise comparisons) could be completed in less than 2 hr using 2 CPUs and <6 GB memory.
evidence: This is a performance benchmark for the software.

claim: The immuneRACE datasets included bulk TCR β-chain repertoires from 694 patients within 0–30 days of COVID-19 diagnosis.
source: The deposited immuneRACE datasets also included bulk TCR β-chain repertoires from 694 patients within 0–30 days of COVID-19 diagnosis.
evidence: This is a description of the data analyzed.

claim: The MIRA assay employed by Nolan et al., 2020 identified TCRs with varying degrees of biochemical similarity.
source: We investigated the degree to which the MIRA assay employed by Nolan et al., 2020 identified TCRs with identical or similar amino acid sequences. In general, across sets of MIRA-identified β-chain TCRs, each associated with a different antigen, the proportion of amino acid sequences observed more than once was generally lower than in the tetramer-enriched repertoires and varied considerably across the sets
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis.

claim: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may be explained by peptides being presented by the full complement of the native host's MHC molecules compared to a single defined peptide–MHC complex.
source: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may, in part, be explained by: (1) peptides being presented by the full complement of the native host's MHC molecules compared to a single defined peptide–MHC complex
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed diversity.

claim: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may be explained by recruitment of lower affinity receptors.
source: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may, in part, be explained by: (1) peptides being presented by the full complement of the native host's MHC molecules compared to a single defined peptide–MHC complex, (2) recruitment of lower affinity receptors
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed diversity.

claim: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may be explained by antigen specificity conferred primarily by the alpha rather than the sequenced beta chain.
source: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may, in part, be explained by: (1) peptides being presented by the full complement of the native host's MHC molecules compared to a single defined peptide–MHC complex, (2) recruitment of lower affinity receptors, (3) antigen specificity conferred primarily by the alpha rather than the sequenced beta chain
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed diversity.

claim: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may be explained by nonspecific 'bystander' activation in the MIRA stimulation assay.
source: The increased diversity in MIRA-enriched TCR sets versus tetramer-enriched TCR sets may, in part, be explained by: (1) peptides being presented by the full complement of the native host's MHC molecules compared to a single defined peptide–MHC complex, (2) recruitment of lower affinity receptors, (3) antigen specificity conferred primarily by the alpha rather than the sequenced beta chain, or (4) nonspecific 'bystander' activation in the MIRA stimulation assay.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed diversity.

claim: TCRs with longer CDR3 loops and lower generation probabilities are likely to have less dense biochemical neighborhoods absent strong selection for antigen recognition.
source: Absent strong selection for antigen recognition, longer TCRs with lower generation probabilities are thus likely to have less dense biochemical neighborhoods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations and prior knowledge.

claim: Biochemical neighborhood density is highly heterogeneous among TCRs and may depend on mechanisms of antigen recognition as well as receptor V(D)J recombination biases.
source: Together, these observations suggest that biochemical neighborhood density is highly heterogeneous among TCRs and that it may depend on mechanisms of antigen recognition as well as receptor V(D)J recombination biases (Thomas and Crawford, 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observations, with citation to prior work.

claim: A limitation of distance-based clustering is the presence of similar TCR sequences that lack the ability to recognize the target antigen.
source: The utility of a TCR-based biomarker depends on the antigen specificity of the TCRs. Therefore, a limitation of distance-based clustering is the presence of similar TCR sequences that lack the ability to recognize the target antigen.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the approach.

claim: A meta-clonotype definition should be broad enough to capture multiple biochemically similar TCRs with shared antigen recognition, but not excessively broad as to include a high proportion of nonspecific TCRs.
source: To be useful, a meta-clonotype definition should be broad enough to capture multiple biochemically similar TCRs with shared antigen recognition, but not excessively broad as to include a high proportion of nonspecific TCRs.
evidence: This is stated as a design principle for meta-clonotypes.

claim: The optimal radius defining a meta-clonotype may differ for each TCR because the density of neighborhoods around TCRs are heterogeneous.
source: Because the density of neighborhoods around TCRs are heterogeneous, we hypothesized that the optimal radius defining a meta-clonotype may differ for each TCR.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The objective is to select the largest radius that includes no more than one in one-million background TCRs.
source: The objective is to select the largest radius that includes no more than one in one-million background TCRs; while this threshold is arbitrary, practically it means that in a deeply sampled repertoire we expect to observe only a few TCRs within the radius and that deviation from this may indicate antigenic selection.
evidence: This is stated as the objective for radius selection.

claim: For each set of antigen-associated TCRs identified using MIRA, a two part background was created consisting of 100,000 synthetic TCRs and 100,000 umbilical cord blood TCRs.
source: Therefore, for each set of antigen-associated TCRs identified using MIRA, we created a two part background. One part consisted of 100,000 synthetic TCRs whose TRBV- and TRBJ-gene frequencies matched those of the antigen-associated TCRs; TCRs were generated using the software OLGA with slight modification to allow V–J gene directed sequence generation (Marcou et al., 2018; Sethna et al., 2019). The other part consisted of 100,000 umbilical cord blood TCRs sampled from 8 subjects (Britanova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: The composition of the background balanced denser sampling of sequences near the candidate meta-clonotype centroids with broad sampling of TCRs from an antigen-naive repertoire.
source: This composition balanced denser sampling of sequences near the candidate meta-clonotype centroids with broad sampling of TCRs from an antigen-naive repertoire.
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for the background composition.

claim: The dense sampling of TCRs with similar V–J combinations to the antigen-associated TCRs allowed for estimation of the overall frequency of meta-clonotype neighbors in the background well below 1 in 200,000.
source: The dense sampling of TCRs with similar V–J combinations to the antigen-associated TCRs allowed for estimation of the overall frequency of meta-clonotype neighbors in the background well below 1 in 200,000.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the sampling approach.

claim: Using 200,000 sequences with V–J-matched sampling strikes a balance between computational efficiency and bias in radius estimates.
source: For large sets of antigen-associated TCRs (i.e., greater than 10,000) or for users with modest computing resources, using 200,000 sequences with V–J-matched sampling strikes a balance between computational efficiency and bias in radius estimates
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The median radius over many iterations using 200,000 sequences coincided with the median radius estimated from a background of 2,000,000 TCRs.
source: using 200,000 sequences with V–J-matched sampling strikes a balance between computational efficiency and bias in radius estimates, where the median radius over many iterations coincided with the median radius estimated from a background of 2,000,000 TCRs.
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Computing radii for 500 unique MIRA TCRs using a synthetic background of 1,000,000 TCRs can be completed in 1 min using 12 CPUs and 48 GB of memory with tcrdist3.
source: For instance, with tcrdist3, computing radii for 500 unique MIRA TCRs using a synthetic background of 1,000,000 TCRs (500,000 synthetic V–J matched and 500,000 sampled from cord blood) can be completed in 1 min using 12 CPUs and 48 GB of memory.
evidence: This is a performance benchmark for the software.

claim: The motif constraint for each radius-defined meta-clonotype was defined by aligning each of the conformant CDR3 amino acid sequences to the centroid CDR3.
source: The motif constraint for each radius-defined meta-clonotype was defined by aligning each of the conformant CDR3 amino acid sequences to the centroid CDR3.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: Alignment positions with five or fewer distinct amino acids were considered conserved and added to the motif as a set of possible residues.
source: Alignment positions with five or fewer distinct amino acids were considered conserved and added to the motif as a set of possible residues.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: The motif constraint is permissive of only specific substitutions in select positions relative to the centroid.
source: Thus, the motif constraint is permissive of only specific substitutions in select positions relative to the centroid, however these substitutions are still penalized by the radius constraint.
evidence: This is a description of how the motif constraint works.

claim: The beta-binomial distribution provided the flexibility needed to adequately fit the TCR data.
source: We found that the beta-binomial distribution, which was recently used for TCR abundance modeling (Rytlewski et al., 2019), provided the flexibility needed to adequately fit the TCR data.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling approach, with citation.

claim: TCR frequencies are count data drawn from samples of heterogeneous size, similar to bulk RNA sequencing data.
source: Similar to bulk RNA sequencing data, TCR frequencies are count data drawn from samples of heterogeneous size.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the data.

claim: The negative binomial model did not adequately fit TCR counts.
source: We found that the negative binomial model did not adequately fit TCR counts, which – compared to transcriptomic data – were characterized by (1) more technical zeros due to inevitable under sampling and (2) even greater biological overdispersion, which could be due to clonal expansions and HLA genotype diversity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the modeling approach.

claim: HLA diversity could be a major hurdle to biomarker development.
source: Though demonstrating HLA restriction of the SARS-CoV-2 meta-clonotypes establishes their potential utility, it also highlighted how HLA diversity could be a major hurdle to biomarker development.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The sensitivity of a TCR-based biomarker in a diverse population may depend on combining meta-clonotypes with diverse HLA restrictions.
source: The sensitivity of a TCR-based biomarker in a diverse population may depend on combining meta-clonotypes with diverse HLA restrictions since individuals with different HLA genotypes often target different epitopes using divergent TCRs.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings.

claim: Having HLA genotype information for TCR repertoire analysis can be critical to interpreting results.
source: Our analysis shows that having HLA genotype information for TCR repertoire analysis can be critical to interpreting results.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: It may be possible to infer high-resolution HLA genotype from bulk TCR repertoires.
source: The simple HLA classifier we developed suggests that soon it may be possible to infer high-resolution HLA genotype from bulk TCR repertoires
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on the classifier developed.

claim: It may be feasible to generate informative TCR meta-clonotypes in the absence of HLA genotype information using a poly-antigenic TCR-enrichment strategy.
source: In the absence of HLA genotype information, it may still be feasible to generate informative TCR meta-clonotypes. For example, a poly-antigenic TCR-enrichment strategy (i.e., peptide pools or whole proteins) could help generate meta-clonotypes that broadly cover HLA diversity if the sample donors are racially, ethnically, and geographically representative of the ultimate target population.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility for future work.

claim: Donor unrestricted T cells and their receptors (e.g., MAITs and γδ T cells) may be good targets for TCR biomarker development.
source: For these reasons, donor unrestricted T cells and their receptors (e.g., MAITs and γδ T cells) may also be good targets for TCR biomarker development.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion for future work.

claim: tcrdist3 is highly flexible, allowing for customization of the distance metric with position and CDR-specific weights and amino acid substitution matrices.
source: The software is highly flexible, allowing for: (1) customization of the distance metric with position and CDR-specific weights and amino acid substitution matrices
evidence: This is a description of the software capabilities.

claim: tcrdist3 allows for inclusion of CDRs beyond the CDR3.
source: The software is highly flexible, allowing for: (1) customization of the distance metric with position and CDR-specific weights and amino acid substitution matrices, (2) inclusion of CDRs beyond the CDR3
evidence: This is a description of the software capabilities.

claim: tcrdist3 allows for clustering based on single-chain or paired-chain data for α/β or γ/δ TCRs.
source: The software is highly flexible, allowing for: (1) customization of the distance metric with position and CDR-specific weights and amino acid substitution matrices, (2) inclusion of CDRs beyond the CDR3, (3) clustering based on single-chain or paired-chain data for α/β or γ/δ TCRs
evidence: This is a description of the software capabilities.

claim: tcrdist3 allows for use of default as well as user-provided TCR repertoires as background for controlling meta-clonotype specificity.
